# Draft:Andrew Johson 1868 presidential campaign

Pre-convention efforts
Johnson failed to secure backing from Northern Democrats.
By late-1867, Johnson had grown frustrated towards many in his party who had refused to endorse him for another term, especially allies of George H. Pendleton.
In December 1867, Johnson sent the U.S. Congress an extraordinary message recommending Winfield Scott Hancock for special commendation. Speculation arose that Johnson was hoping to raise Hancock's possible profile as a contender for the nomination, in hopes of blocking Pendleton and others from the nomination, and hopefully raising his own path to the nomination.
Defeat at convention
Heading into the 1868 Democratic National Convention in New York in July 1868, Johnson remained very popular among Southern whites. He had boosted that popularity by issuing, just before the convention, a pardon ending the possibility of criminal proceedings against any Confederate not already indicted, meaning that only Davis and a few others still might face trial. The report of the 1868 impeachment managers investigation into possible corruption in support of Johnson during his impeachment trial was released one week before the convention, with impeachment manager Benjamin Butler hoping its release would harm Johnson's odds of securing his party's nomination.
On the first ballot, Johnson was second to former Ohio representative George H. Pendleton, who had been his Democratic opponent for vice president in 1864. Johnson's support was mostly from the South, and fell away as the ballots passed. On the 22nd ballot, former New York governor Horatio Seymour was nominated, and the President received only four votes (all from Tennessee delegates).
